extracted.intended_audience: readers and supporters of The Forerunner; women interested in suffrage, social reform, small-scale entrepreneurs and magazine editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for producing, evaluating, and sustaining a small progressive women's periodical and related social advocacy (including magazine presentation, finances, recommended content, and related practical/social guidance for readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cafeteria/lunch_business success factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide good food, cheapness, comfortable seating and a chance for talk and a smoke; self-service counter where patrons take what they like; use of wholesale purchasing and organized kitchen staff to keep prices low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diantha's 'Caffeteria' attracted patrons because it combined 'good food, cheapness, a chance for a comfortable seat and talk and a smoke.' Operational signs of success included: high turnover (workers taking lunches), low per-item prices (sandwiches five cents, coffee five cents, cakes two for five), fresh home-baked bread and rolls, wholesale buying to reduce cost, and multiple staff roles (cook, helper, assistant). The text emphasizes volume, organization, quality of basic items (real bread, cream in coffee) and efficient use of house resources to be profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small food-business pricing and product quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep prices very low while maintaining clear quality of staples (perfect bread, excellent butter, good coffee) to drive volume and ancillary sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete price/quality example in the narrative: six sandwiches for five cents, cup of coffee five cents, drop cakes two for five; patrons noticed lack of scum on milk, real bread, and distinctive sandwich fillings. Guidance implies profit comes from wholesale input purchasing and baking in large quantities daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing a house-workers' cooperative/union
rubrics_metrics.description: Select, train and employ house-workers with agreed hours and pay; provide living accommodations and reasonable leisure space as part of employment terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model described: a House Worker's Union of thirty girls, 'picked and trained'; previously working out as servants and receiving six dollars a week 'and found'; then reorganized to be paid by hour or day and 'found' themselves; each worker has her own room and access to porches and ballroom except for scheduled events. Emphasizes organization, training, fair pay, and decent living/working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of an effective women's magazine (presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine women's publication should be big, handsome and dignified, printed in large clear type on good paper, and substantial in size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer praises The Englishwoman as 'a big, handsome, dignified monthly; 120 pages in large clear type... paper, a joy to the hand.' Even without pictures, good use of type and paper weight enhances reader experience. Physical production values are part of the magazine's quality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of an effective women's magazine (editorial/content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide breadth of view, excellent writers, varied material affecting women's affairs, and coverage beyond a single cause (e.g., suffrage) to make a magazine broadly useful and persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Englishwoman is commended for 'breadth of view' and giving 'studies... of the previous position of women, of her place in different countries and classes, of her connection with the other stirring questions of the day.' Good magazines emphasize both specialised causes (the ballot) and wider context; attract excellent writers and present material 'good reading straight through.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a movement's official organ
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization's official journal should be representative, have wide support, and serve as a reliable channel for the movement's discourse and information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Woman's Journal 'is now the official organ of the National American Woman suffrage association'—the association needs an organ, and the paper needs and desired a wider support than the movement previously gave it. Implies criteria: institutional endorsement, consistent publication schedule (weekly/monthly), and broad circulation among supporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine financial sustainability (subscriber target)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small magazine must reach a minimum subscriber base to cover running expenses; Forerunner needs about three thousand subscribers as a bare minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial states the magazine currently has 1,100–1,200 subscribers and 'must have about three thousand subscribers' to pay running expenses (providing no salary to the editor). This is explicit financial threshold guidance for editors/publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective public-health advocacy article standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear data to identify preventable causes, quantify their contribution, and compare demographic/setting differences to argue for public awareness and policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Dr. Salmon's article: shows numbers (30,456 patients, 5,301 new admissions), identifies '664 cases of general paralysis (dependant on syphilis) and 638 cases of alcoholic psychoses' and notes urban-versus-rural differences and percentage breakdowns ('42 per cent. of all male admissions from cities were for general paralysis and the alcoholic psychoses'). The text suggests effective advocacy pairs solid statistics with a call for social awakening and preventive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a National Department of Health (Owen Bill duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national health department should safeguard pure food, pure drugs, pure streams, and study and maintain human health, without regulating the practice of medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece defines the Owen Bill's aims: focus on public health measures (pure food/drugs/streams) and study human health; it explicitly notes the Bill 'does not seek to regulate the practice of medicine.' The department is compared to the Bureau of Agriculture in safeguarding livestock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for civic legal education
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be simple, taught in schools, and explained so that a child of ten could rewrite the main features of the laws of his country, state, and city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that 'a child of ten should be considered grossly uneducated who could not rewrite the main features of the laws of his country' and provides sample teacher–child Q&A to illustrate how laws and taxes might be taught. Emphasizes simplicity, pedagogy, and democratization of legal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of democratic government (normative standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracy, law and government should evolve from the people and represent the common good; government should be service-oriented (co-ordination and agreement) rather than compulsion, and laws should be based on sociology and constructive principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts masculine, coercive models of government with the desired human/democratic model: 'In a Democracy Law and Government both change... government ceases to be compulsion, and becomes agreement; law ceases to be authority and becomes co-ordination.' It urges simplification of laws and education of citizens, and treating government as public service rather than spoils to be taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument for women's participation in government (descriptive standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women bring feminine features—care, nurture, provision, education derived from motherhood—which make them especially fit for the administration of constructive social interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reasons that 'Government by women, so far as it is influenced by their sex, would be influenced by motherhood; and that would mean care, nurture, provision, education,' citing social insect models (ants, bees) as examples of organized maternal sociality. This is presented as a normative criterion for evaluating the effects of women's suffrage and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics for confronting academic bias against women
rubrics_metrics.description: Counteract stereotypes by proving difference through individual conduct and excellence—'show them the difference in human personality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to a student complaining of professors who mark women lower: 'The way to start... is to prove that they are not [cast from the same mold] by being different.' The guidance implies consistent performance, distinctive individuality and personal influence as means to combat biased generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization strategy for married women to continue professional work
rubrics_metrics.description: Political organization and securing equal suffrage is the appropriate strategy for married women to protect and continue professional practice (e.g., teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In response to married women losing teaching opportunities, the answer given is straightforward: 'The most suitable organization... is political organization... by securing equal suffrage.' Presents suffrage as structural remedy rather than ad hoc workplace tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette for shared social expenses (dating/mixed company)
rubrics_metrics.description: If he invites, he pays for both; if she invites, she pays for both; if each takes separate initiative, each pays for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered as a practical arrangement between a man and a woman who wish to associate as equals: concrete rule for social expenses intended to avoid awkwardness and assert equality while preserving social niceties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal-survival financial tactics for an exhausted single woman
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical earning options include taking in washing, sewing/mending, making & selling a specialty product, taking boarders, doing housework for a fixed period to raise funds, or cultivating food if there's land—combined with planning ahead and enlarging intellectual life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advice to a thirty-year-old single woman: list of concrete options (washing, sewing, making one thing well and selling it, boarding, housework to earn $150 in six months, raising some food) plus psychological guidance (plan ahead, broaden interests, bear current trouble with hope for the future). The response gives both immediate practical routes and longer-term mental strategies for coping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic conduct when condemned (moral/legal stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a good citizen, one should submit peacefully to legal execution rather than resist violently (Socratic standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer to the question about a person condemned to die for a crime he did not commit: 'As a good citizen he should submit. See Socrates.' This states a moral/legal criterion prioritizing peaceful submission to the rule of law over violent resistance.
